name: Hebrews
sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The chief early witnesses are the papyrus P46 (about AD 200), which places Hebrews among Paul’s letters directly after Romans, the papyrus P13 (3rd–4th century), and Codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Vaticanus (4th–5th century); Vaticanus breaks off at 9:14. Where manuscript readings are cited in the notes, they are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. *Christos* is rendered “Christ” where it functions as part of Jesus’ name. Old Testament quotations generally follow the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint); where they quote a passage that has the divine name in Hebrew, “Lord” renders Greek *kyrios* and a note gives *Yahweh*. Authorship: the work names no author. Eastern churches from the late 2nd century linked it with Paul, while Tertullian named Barnabas, and Origen remarked that “who wrote the letter, God truly knows.” Other proposals include Apollos, Luke, Silvanus and Priscilla. The writer knew Timothy (13:23) and had heard the message from those who heard the Lord (2:3). Its date is uncertain, though many place it before AD 96, when 1 Clement appears to use it. The question of authorship remains open.

verses.text: In many portions and in many ways God spoke long ago to our ancestors through the prophets,{a}
but in these last days he has spoken to us through a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things and through whom he also made the ages.{b}

He is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact imprint of his very being, and he bears up all things by his mighty word. After he had made purification for sins, he took his seat at the right hand of the Majesty on high,{c}
So he has come to rank as far above the angels as the name he has received as his inheritance surpasses theirs.

And when, again, he leads the firstborn into the inhabited world, he declares,
“All the angels of God must bow down before him.”{f}

These will come to ruin, but you continue;
like clothing, every one of them will grow old.

You will roll them up like a cloak,
and like a garment they will be changed.
But you are the same,
and your years will never come to an end.”{j}
Are they not all spirits in holy service, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are going to inherit salvation?{l}

notes.text: Our ancestors: literally “the fathers.”
In these last days: literally “at the end of these days.” *The ages*: or “the universe,” “the worlds.”

Radiance: or “reflection.” *Exact imprint*: Greek *charaktēr*, the mark stamped on a coin or seal. *Purification for sins*: later manuscripts read “purification for our sins by himself.” *Took his seat … at the right hand*: echoing Ps 110:1.
Ps 2:7. *I have become your Father*: literally “I have begotten you.”
Deut 32:43 in the Greek Old Testament (not in the standard Hebrew text, but compare a Hebrew copy among the Dead Sea Scrolls); compare Ps 97:7. *Again, when he brings*: or “when he again brings.”
Ps 104:4 in the Greek Old Testament. *Winds*: or “spirits”; the same Greek word means both.

Ps 45:6–7. *Your throne, O God, is*: or “God is your throne.” *Forever and ever*: Westcott and Hort bracket “and ever.” *His kingdom*: so the Westcott–Hort text, following P46, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus as reported; most manuscripts read “your kingdom.”
Ps 102:25–27 in the Greek Old Testament. *Lord*: the Greek Old Testament adds this word; in the Hebrew psalm the one addressed is Yahweh (verses 12, 19).
Like a garment: these words are not in the psalm; P46, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Vaticanus as reported include them here, while later manuscripts omit them.
Spirits in holy service: literally “ministering spirits.”

verses.text: For this reason it is all the more necessary for us to hold on to the things we have heard, or we may be carried off course.
For if the message spoken through angels proved valid, and every violation and disobedience received its just penalty,{a}
how will we escape if we neglect a salvation as great as this? It was first spoken by the Lord, and it was confirmed to us by those who heard him,
while God added his own testimony by signs and wonders and various miracles, and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed as he willed.
It was not to angels, after all, that he made subject the coming world we are speaking about.

For a little while you made him lower than the angels;
you crowned him with glory and honor;{c}

all things you have placed beneath his feet.”
In subjecting all things to him, he has left nothing outside his rule. Yet at present we do not see all things made subject to him.

What we do see is Jesus, made for a short time lower than the angels, and now, on account of the death he suffered, wearing a crown of glory and honor, so that by God’s grace he might taste death on behalf of every one.{d}
It was right that God, the one for whose sake and by whose agency everything exists, should bring the founder of their salvation to completion through sufferings, as he leads many sons into glory.{e}
For the one who makes holy and those who are made holy all have one origin. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers,{f}

Since, then, the children share in flesh and blood, he too likewise took part in the same things, so that through death he might break the power of the one who holds the power of death, that is, the devil,{j}
and set free all those who through fear of death were held in slavery all their lives.
For surely it is not angels he takes hold of to help, but he takes hold of the descendants of Abraham.{k}
So it was necessary for him to become like his brothers in all things, in order to be a high priest merciful and faithful in what concerns God, making atonement for the people’s sins.{l}
Because he himself suffered when he was tested, he is able to help those who are being tested.{m}

notes.text: The message spoken through angels: Jewish tradition held that angels took part in the giving of the law at Sinai; compare Deut 33:2 in the Greek Old Testament; Acts 7:53; Gal 3:19.
Ps 8:4–6 in the Greek Old Testament. *Man … son of man*: a human being, humankind. In verses 8–9 the writer applies the psalm to Jesus.

For a little while: or “a little.” The Hebrew of Ps 8:5 reads “a little lower than God” (or “than divine beings”). *Honor*: later manuscripts add “and set him over the works of your hands”; Westcott and Hort bracket these words.

*Jesus*: the Greek form of Hebrew *Yeshua* (Joshua), “Yahweh saves.” *By the grace of God*: so nearly all manuscripts. A few manuscripts, and some writers known to Origen in the 3rd century, read *chōris theou*, “apart from God,” instead of *chariti theou*, “by the grace of God.” The rarer reading is defended by some scholars as the harder one; most editors follow the reading in the text.
Sons: including daughters; the Greek uses the masculine plural for a mixed group. *Founder*: Greek *archēgos*, “leader,” “pioneer,” “trailblazer.” *Bring … to completion*: or “make perfect.”
One origin: literally “are all from one,” that is, from one Father, or from one family. *Brothers*: Greek *adelphoi*, which includes sisters when used of a group; so throughout.
Ps 22:22. *Assembly*: Greek *ekklēsia*, the word usually rendered “church.”
Isa 8:17 in the Greek Old Testament; compare 2 Sam 22:3.
The devil: Greek *diabolos*, “slanderer.”
Takes hold of: or “gives help to.” *Descendants*: literally “seed.” *Abraham*: Hebrew, explained in Gen 17:5 as “father of a multitude.”
Making atonement for: or “making propitiation for,” “wipe away.”
Tested: or “tempted”; the same Greek word covers both.

verses.text: So then, holy brothers, who share in a heavenly calling, fix your thoughts on Jesus, the apostle and high priest of the faith we confess.{a}
He has been faithful to the one who appointed him, as Moses too was faithful in all his house.{b}
But Jesus has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, in the way that the one who builds a house is held in higher honor than the house.
Every house has its builder, and the one who built all things is God.
Moses indeed was faithful in all God’s house, as an attendant, bearing witness to the things that were going to be spoken,{c}
but Christ is faithful as a Son set over God’s house; and that house is ourselves, provided we keep firm hold of our boldness and of the hope that is our boast.{d}

Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says,
“Today, if you hear his voice,

do not make your hearts hard as they did at the Provocation,
at the time of the Testing in the desert,{e}

where your ancestors put me to the test by trying me,
though they saw my works for forty years.

So in my wrath I swore an oath:
‘Into my rest they shall not come.’ ”{f}
Take care, brothers, that none of you has an evil, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.
Rather, keep urging one another on, day by day, for as long as there is a “today,” so that sin’s deceit may harden none of you.
For we have come to share in Christ, provided that we keep the confidence we had at the start unshaken to the last.{g}

In the words of Scripture,
“Today, if you should hear his voice,
do not make your hearts hard as they did at the Provocation.”
Who were they who heard and yet rebelled? Was it not all those who came out of Egypt led by Moses?
And with whom was God angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?{h}
To whom did he swear that they would never come into his rest? Was it not to those who refused to obey?
And we see that unbelief kept them from coming in.

notes.text: Apostle: Greek *apostolos*, “one sent.” *Jesus*: later manuscripts read “Christ Jesus.” *Christ*: Greek *Christos*, “Anointed One,” equivalent to Hebrew *mashiach*, “Messiah.”

*Moses*: Hebrew *Mosheh*, explained in Exod 2:10 as “drawn out”; it may come from an Egyptian word for “son.” *In all God’s house*: Num 12:7 in the Greek Old Testament; literally “in all his house.” Westcott and Hort bracket “all”; P13, P46 and Vaticanus as reported omit it.
Attendant: Greek *therapōn*, an attendant, from Num 12:7.
*Hope that is our boast*: later manuscripts add “firm to the end”; Westcott and Hort bracket these words, which P13, P46 and Vaticanus as reported omit (compare verse 14).
Ps 95:7–11 in the Greek Old Testament. *The rebellion … testing*: in Hebrew these are the place names *Meribah*, “quarreling,” and *Massah*, “testing” (Exod 17:7; Num 20:13).
They shall not come: literally “if they shall enter,” a Hebrew form of oath meaning “they shall not enter.”
Come to share in Christ: or “become partners of Christ.” *Confidence*: Greek *hypostasis*, “assurance,” “resolve”; compare 1:3; 11:1.
Whose bodies fell: compare Num 14:29, 32.

verses.text: Since, then, the promise of entering his rest still stands, let us be wary that none of you should seem to have fallen short of it.
For good news has been brought to us as well as to them. Yet the word they heard was of no benefit to them, because they were not joined in faith with those who truly listened.{a}

For we who have believed are entering that rest, just as he has said,
“So I swore in my anger,
‘They shall never enter my rest,’ ”
although his works had been finished since the foundation of the world.{b}
For in one place he speaks of the seventh day like this: “God rested from all his works on the seventh day.”{c}
And again in this passage he says, “They shall never enter my rest.”
It still remains, then, that some are to come into it, and since those to whom the good news came first did not come in, because they would not obey,
Had Joshua given them rest, God would not afterward have spoken of a further day.{e}
So then, a sabbath rest remains for the people of God;{f}
for anyone who has come into God’s rest has ceased from his labors, just as God ceased from his own.
So let us be earnest to come into that rest, so that none of us falls through the same kind of disobedience they showed.

For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing as far as the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
No creature is hidden from his sight, but all things are bare and laid open to the eyes of the one to whom we must give account.{g}
Since, then, we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast the faith we confess.
Ours is not a high priest who cannot feel for us in our frailties; he has been put to the test in all things just as we are, yet without sinning.
So let us draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us at the moment of need.

notes.text: Because they were not united in faith with those who listened: so the Westcott–Hort text, with most early manuscripts as reported. Some manuscripts read “because it was not combined with faith in those who heard it.”
Gen 2:2.
*David*: Hebrew, probably “beloved.” The Greek Old Testament gives Psalm 95 a heading naming David.
*Joshua*: Hebrew *Yehoshua*, “Yahweh saves”; the Greek name is *Iēsous*, the same as “Jesus.”
Sabbath rest: Greek *sabbatismos*, “sabbath-keeping”; *sabbath* is Hebrew for “ceasing,” “rest.”
Laid open: literally “with the neck bent back,” exposed. *To whom we must give account*: or “with whom we have to do.”

verses.text: Every high priest is chosen from among men and appointed to act on their behalf in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.
He is able to deal gently with the ignorant and the wayward, since he himself is beset by weakness.
and for that reason he has to bring an offering for sins on his own account as well as on behalf of the people.
And no one takes this honor on himself; he must be called by God, just as Aaron was.{a}

During his life in the flesh he offered prayers and earnest requests, with a loud outcry and with tears, to the one who had power to rescue him from death, and he was heard because of his devotion.{d}
Son though he was, he learned obedience from the things he suffered.{e}
And once made complete, he became for all who obey him the cause of salvation that lasts forever,
since God designated him a high priest in the order of Melchizedek.
On this subject we have a great deal to say, and it is difficult to make clear, because you have grown dull of hearing.
By now you should be teaching others, yet you need someone to teach you once more the basic rudiments of the sayings of God. You have come to need milk rather than solid food.{f}
For everyone who lives on milk is unacquainted with the message of righteousness, being still an infant.
But solid food belongs to the mature, to those whose faculties have been trained by practice to tell good from evil.

notes.text: *Aaron*: Hebrew, of uncertain meaning; Moses’ brother and the first high priest (Exod 28:1).

Ps 110:4. *Melchizedek*: Hebrew, “my king is righteousness” or “king of righteousness” (7:2); the king and priest of Salem who blessed Abraham (Gen 14:18–20). *In the order of*: or “after the manner of.”
Because of his devotion: or “because of his reverent fear”; others render “and was delivered from his fear.”
He learned … he suffered: Greek *emathen … epathen*, a play on words.
Basic rudiments: or “first principles,” literally “the elements of the beginning.”

verses.text: So let us leave behind the elementary teaching about Christ and press on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith in God,{a}
teaching about washings and the laying on of hands, about the raising of the dead and the judgment that lasts forever.{b}
And this we will do, if God permits.
There is no way, when people have once received the light, have tasted the gift from heaven, have come to share in the Holy Spirit,
who have tasted the goodness of God’s word and the powers of the age to come,
and then have fallen away, to bring them back to repentance again; for they are crucifying the Son of God afresh to their own ruin, and making a public mockery of him.{c}
Ground that soaks up the rain falling on it time after time, and brings forth plants of use to those for whom it is worked, has a share in God’s blessing.
But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and close to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.{d}
Even though we speak this way, dear friends, we are confident of better things in your case, things that go with salvation.
For God is not unjust; he will not forget your work and the love you showed for his name in serving the saints, as you still serve them.{e}
And we long for each one of you to show the same eagerness for the full assurance of hope until the end,
so that you may not become sluggish, but imitate those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
When God gave his promise to Abraham, he swore by himself, because there was no one greater for him to swear by,
saying, “Surely I will bless you and multiply you.”{f}
And so Abraham, having waited with patience, received what was promised.
People swear by someone greater than themselves, and for them an oath serves as confirmation and puts an end to every dispute.
In the same way, God, wanting to show the heirs of the promise even more plainly that his purpose could not change, guaranteed it with an oath,
so that through two things that cannot change, in which God cannot possibly lie, we who have taken refuge might be strongly encouraged to lay hold of the hope that lies before us.
This hope we hold as the soul’s anchor, firm and secure, and it goes in to the inner place beyond the curtain,{g}
where Jesus has entered for us as a forerunner, having become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.

notes.text: The elementary teaching about Christ: literally “the word of the beginning of the Christ.” *Maturity*: or “perfection,” “completion.”

Teaching about washings: so the Westcott–Hort text, following Vaticanus as reported (“a foundation … teaching”); most manuscripts read “of teaching about washings.” *Washings*: Greek *baptismoi*, “baptisms,” “ritual washings.”
For they are crucifying: or “while they are crucifying.” *Afresh*: or “for themselves”; the Greek *anastaurountas* can mean either.
Thorns and thistles: compare Gen 3:17–18.
Saints: literally “holy ones,” that is, God’s people.
Gen 22:17. *Surely I will bless you and multiply you*: literally “blessing I will bless you and multiplying I will multiply you.”
The inner place beyond the curtain: the inmost room of the sanctuary, the Most Holy Place (Lev 16:2, 12).

verses.text: For this Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, went out to meet Abraham when he came back from the slaughter of the kings, and he blessed him;{a}
and Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. His name means first “king of righteousness,” and then he is also king of Salem, that is, “king of peace.”
He is without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life; but, made like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time.{b}
See how great this man was, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils.

Now the descendants of Levi who take on the priestly office are commanded by the law to take tithes from the people, that is, from their own brothers, even though these also are offspring of Abraham.{c}
But this man, whose ancestry is not traced from them, took tithes from Abraham and gave a blessing to the man who held the promises.
Beyond any dispute, the lesser is blessed by the greater.
In the one case, tithes are received by men who die; in the other, by one of whom it is testified that he lives.
One might even say that Levi, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham,
for he was still in the body of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.{d}

If, then, the Levitical priesthood could have brought about perfection, for it was in connection with it that the people were given the law, why was there still need for a different priest to arise in the line of Melchizedek, and not one designated in the line of Aaron?
For when the priesthood is changed, a change of law necessarily follows as well.
The one these things are spoken of belonged to another tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar.
For it is evident that our Lord arose from Judah, and Moses said nothing about priests in connection with that tribe.{e}
And this becomes still more evident when another priest arises who resembles Melchizedek,
one who has become priest, not by virtue of a rule about bodily descent, but by virtue of the power of a life that cannot be destroyed.{f}

For the testimony is,
“A priest you are forever,
in the line of Melchizedek.”
On the one hand, an earlier command is set aside because it was weak and useless,
for the law brought nothing to completion. In its place a better hope is brought in, and by it we come near to God.
And it did not happen without an oath. Others became priests without an oath,

but this one became priest on oath, when God declared to him,
“The Lord has taken an oath
and will not go back on it:
‘A priest you are forever.’ ”{g}
To that same degree Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant.
Furthermore, the former priests were many in number, because death prevented them from continuing in office;
He, however, because he lives on forever, holds a priesthood that does not pass to another.
That is why he can save for all time those who come to God by him; he is always alive to plead on their behalf.{h}
It was fitting that we should have such a high priest: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens.
He has no need, as those high priests do, to offer sacrifices day after day, first for his own sins and then for those of the people; for he did this once for all when he offered up himself.
For the law appoints as high priests men who are subject to weakness, but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever.

notes.text: *Salem*: Hebrew, “peace”; usually identified with Jerusalem (Ps 76:2). *God Most High*: Hebrew *El Elyon*. See Gen 14:17–20.
Without father … genealogy: Genesis records no parents, ancestry, birth or death for him.
*Levi*: Hebrew, explained in Gen 29:34 as “attached.” *Descended from*: literally “have come out of the loins of.”
In the body of his ancestor: literally “in the loins of his father.”
*Judah*: Hebrew, explained in Gen 29:35 as “praise.” *Arose*: the Greek verb is used of the rising of a star or the springing up of a plant; compare Isa 11:1; Jer 23:5.
A rule about bodily descent: literally “a law of a fleshly commandment.”
Ps 110:4. *The Lord*: the Hebrew text has *Yahweh*. *Forever*: later manuscripts add “in the order of Melchizedek.”
For all time: or “completely.”

verses.text: The chief point of what we are saying is this: we have a high priest of this kind, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven,
a minister in the sanctuary and in the true tent, which the Lord set up, not any human being.{a}
For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices, so it is necessary for this one too to have something to offer.
Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are already priests who offer the gifts according to the law.

They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, just as Moses was warned when he was about to erect the tent: “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.”{b}
As it is, however, the ministry Christ has received is far more excellent, to the same degree that the covenant of which he is mediator is better, resting as it does on better promises.
Had nothing been wrong with that first covenant, no place would have been sought for a second one.

For he finds fault with them when he says,
“Look, the days are coming, says the Lord,
when I will establish a new covenant
with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.{c}

For this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel
when those days are over, says the Lord:
I will place my laws in their understanding,
and inscribe them upon their hearts;
I will be God to them,
and they will be a people to me.

No longer will each one teach his fellow townsman,
or each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord.’
For all of them will know me,
from the smallest to the greatest.{e}

For I will be merciful toward their wrongdoings,
and I will remember their sins no more.”{f}
When he says “new,” he has made the first covenant old; and what is growing old and aging will soon disappear.

notes.text: The sanctuary: literally “the holy things” or “the holy places.” *Tent*: or “tabernacle,” the portable sanctuary of Israel in the wilderness; compare Num 24:6 in the Greek Old Testament.
Exod 25:40.
Jer 31:31–34 (38:31–34 in the Greek Old Testament). *The Lord*: the Hebrew text has *Yahweh*; so also in verses 9–10. *Israel*: Hebrew, explained in Gen 32:28 as “he struggles with God.”
I too disregarded them: so the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew reads “though I was a husband to them.”
Know the Lord: the Hebrew text has *Yahweh*.
Their sins: later manuscripts add “and their lawless deeds,” as in 10:17.

verses.text: The first covenant, for its part, had rules for worship and a sanctuary belonging to this world.{a}
For a tent was prepared, the first room, in which were the lampstand, the table and the bread of the presence; this is called the Holy Place.{b}
Behind the second curtain was the room called the Most Holy Place,{c}

which had the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant, covered with gold on all sides. In the ark were a golden jar holding the manna, Aaron’s staff that had sprouted, and the tablets of the covenant.{d}
and over it the cherubim of the Glory cast their shadow over the mercy seat. We cannot speak about these things one by one at present.{e}
With these things arranged in this way, the priests go regularly into the first room in performing their duties,
Into the second room, however, the high priest alone goes, only once a year, and always with blood, which he brings as an offering for himself and for the sins of the people done in ignorance.{f}
The Holy Spirit is making it plain by this that the way into the sanctuary has not yet been opened as long as the first tent still has its standing.
This is a figure pointing to the present time. Under it gifts and sacrifices are brought that have no power to make the worshiper perfect in conscience,{g}
dealing only with foods and drinks and different kinds of washing. These are outward rules for the body, in force until the time comes to set things straight.
But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have now come, then through the greater and more perfect tent, not made with hands, that is, not of this creation,{h}
he entered once for all into the sanctuary, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, and obtained eternal redemption.
For if the blood of goats and bulls and the sprinkled ashes of a heifer sanctify those who are defiled, so that their flesh is made clean,{i}
how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God!{j}

For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who have been called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has taken place that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.
In the case of a will, it is necessary to establish that the one who made it has died.{k}
A will is valid only once someone has died; it has no force as long as the one who made it is still living.
That is why not even the first covenant was put into effect without blood.

For when every command of the law had been spoken by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people,{l}
saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God has commanded for you.”{m}
Likewise he sprinkled blood on the tent and on every vessel used in the ministry.
In fact, under the law nearly everything is made clean with blood, and apart from the pouring out of blood there is no forgiveness.
It was necessary, then, for the copies of the things in heaven to be cleansed by such means, but the heavenly things themselves needed better sacrifices than these.
Christ did not go into a holy place made by human hands, a copy of the real one; he went into heaven itself, to appear now before God’s face for us.
Nor was it to offer himself many times over, as the high priest goes into the holy place each year with blood that is not his own;
if that were so, he would have needed to suffer many times since the world was founded. Instead he has been revealed once, at the end of the ages, to do away with sin by sacrificing himself.
And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after that comes judgment,
so also Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to bring salvation to those who are eagerly waiting for him.{n}

notes.text: For its part: Westcott and Hort bracket the word “also” (or “even”) here. *A sanctuary belonging to this world*: or “an earthly sanctuary.”
The bread of the presence: literally “the setting out of the loaves” (Exod 25:30; Lev 24:5–9).
The Most Holy Place: literally “the holy of holies.”

Altar of incense: or “censer”; the Greek *thymiatērion* can mean either. In Exodus the incense altar stood in front of the curtain (Exod 30:6). *Manna*: Hebrew, explained in Exod 16:15, 31 from the question “What is it?” See Exod 16:33; Num 17:8–10; Deut 10:1–5.
Cherubim: Hebrew plural of *cherub*, winged heavenly beings. *Mercy seat*: Greek *hilastērion*, the gold lid of the ark, “place of atonement” (Exod 25:17–22).
Once a year: on the Day of Atonement (Lev 16), in the seventh month (September–October), on its tenth day.
Figure: Greek *parabolē*, “parable,” “figure.”
That have now come: so the Westcott–Hort text, with P46 and Vaticanus as reported; many manuscripts read “that are to come.”
Ashes of a heifer: see Num 19:1–10, 17–19.
Our conscience: so the Westcott–Hort text; many manuscripts read “your conscience.” *The eternal Spirit*: or “an eternal spirit.”
Will: the Greek *diathēkē* means both “covenant” and “will” (“testament”), and the writer plays on both senses in verses 15–18.
Hyssop: a small aromatic plant used for sprinkling. Compare Exod 24:3–8. *Calves and goats*: some manuscripts read only “calves.”
Exod 24:8.
To bear the sins of many: echoing Isa 53:12.

verses.text: The law holds only a shadow of the good things that were to come, not the very form of those realities. So by the same sacrifices, offered without end year by year, it can never make perfect those who come forward to worship.{a}
If they could, would the offering of them not have come to an end, since those who worship, once made clean, would have no further awareness of sins?
Instead, these sacrifices bring sins to mind again every year,
since the blood of bulls and goats cannot possibly take sins away.

in offerings burned whole and in offerings for sin
you found no pleasure.

Then I said, ‘Here I am; I have come,
as it stands written of me in the scroll of the book,
to do your will, O God.’ ”
First he says, “Sacrifices and offerings, whole burnt offerings and sin offerings you did not want and took no pleasure in,” though these are offered according to the law.
Then he adds, “Here I am; I have come to do your will.” He sets aside the first in order to establish the second.
And it is by that will that we have been made holy, through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
Every priest, moreover, stands daily performing his ministry, presenting over and over the identical sacrifices, which are never able to remove sins.{c}
But this one, having offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, sat down at God’s right hand,{d}
and from then on he waits until his enemies are made a footstool for his feet.{e}
For by a single offering he has made perfect for all time those who are being made holy.
And the Holy Spirit testifies to us as well. For after he has said,

“This is the covenant I will make with them
when those days are over, says the Lord:
I will place my laws on their hearts,
and inscribe them upon their minds,”{f}

he goes on,
“Their sins and their lawless acts
I will call to mind no more.”
Where these have been forgiven, there is no longer any offering for sin.
So then, brothers, since by Jesus’ blood we have boldness to go into the holy place,
by a way newly made and living, which he has opened up for us through the curtain, which is his flesh,
and since we have a great priest over the house of God,
let us come near with a true heart, in the full assurance that faith gives, our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.
Let us keep hold of the hope we confess without wavering, for the one who gave the promise can be trusted.
And let us take thought for one another, how to stir each other up to love and good works,
not giving up meeting together, as is the custom of some, but urging each other on, and doing so the more as you see the Day drawing near.{g}
If we keep on sinning willfully once we have come to know the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains any longer,
but only a terrifying expectation of judgment, and a raging fire that will consume the adversaries.{h}
Whoever rejected the law of Moses was put to death without pity, when two or three witnesses gave evidence.{i}
Think how much more severe a penalty will be due to one who has spurned the Son of God, has counted as unclean the covenant blood by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace.{j}
We know who it is that said, “Retribution belongs to me; I will pay back,” and again, “The Lord will judge his people.”{k}
It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
But call to mind the former days, when, after you had received the light, you endured a hard contest of sufferings.
At times you were publicly exposed to insults and afflictions; at other times you stood alongside those who were treated in that way.
For you shared the sufferings of the prisoners, and you accepted with joy the seizure of your possessions, knowing that you yourselves had a better possession, and a lasting one.{l}
So do not throw away your confidence, which carries a great reward.
For you need to persevere, so that, having done what God wills, you may receive the promise.
We, however, are not people who draw back to their ruin, but people of faith who hold on to their souls.{o}

notes.text: The very form: literally “the image itself.”
Ps 40:6–8 in the Greek Old Testament. *A body you have made ready for me*: so the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew reads “ears you have dug for me,” that is, “you have opened my ears.”
Every priest: some manuscripts read “every high priest.”
For all time: or, taken with what follows, “sat down for all time.”
Jer 31:33–34. *The Lord*: the Hebrew text has *Yahweh*.
The Day: the day of the Lord’s coming and judgment.
Raging fire: literally “zeal of fire”; compare Isa 26:11.
Compare Deut 17:6.
Counted as unclean: or “treated as common.” Compare Exod 24:8.
Deut 32:35–36. *The Lord*: the Hebrew text has *Yahweh*. *I will repay*: later manuscripts add “says the Lord.”
The prisoners: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Alexandrinus as reported; later manuscripts read “my chains.” *You yourselves had*: later manuscripts add “in heaven.”
In just a little while: literally “a little, how very little,” from Isa 26:20. The rest of verses 37–38 is from Hab 2:3–4 in the Greek Old Testament.
My righteous one: Westcott and Hort bracket “my”; some manuscripts place it after “faith” (“will live by my faith”), and later manuscripts omit it.
Hold on to their souls: or “gain their lives.”

verses.text: Faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen.{a}
For it was for this that the elders of long ago were commended.{b}
By faith we understand that the ages were set in order by God’s word, so that what is seen did not come into being out of things that appear.{c}
By faith Abel offered to God a sacrifice greater than Cain’s. Through this he was declared righteous, since God gave testimony over his gifts; and through it, though dead, he speaks still.{d}
By faith Enoch was taken away so that he did not see death, and “he was not found, because God had taken him.” For before he was taken, it was attested of him that he had pleased God.{e}
And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever draws near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.

By faith Noah, when he had been divinely warned about things as yet unseen, reverently prepared an ark for the rescue of his family. Through his faith he passed sentence on the world, and he became heir to the righteousness that accords with faith.{f}
By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place he was going to receive as an inheritance, and he went out without knowing where he was going.
By faith he lived as a foreigner in the land of promise, as in a land not his own, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise.{g}
He was awaiting the city with firm foundations, whose architect and maker is God.
By faith Sarah herself, too, received power to conceive offspring, even beyond the age for it, since she judged the one who had promised to be faithful.{h}
And so from one man, and he as good as dead, there came descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as countless as the grains of sand on the seashore.{i}
These all died in faith without having received the promises, but they saw them and greeted them from afar, and they confessed that they were strangers and exiles on the earth.{j}
People who speak this way make it clear that they are looking for a homeland.
If they had been thinking of the land they had left behind, they would have had opportunity to return.
But as it is, they long for a better country, a heavenly one. That is why God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.
By faith Abraham, when tested, offered Isaac as a sacrifice. The man who had welcomed the promises was offering up his one and only son,{k}
the one of whom it had been said, “Through Isaac your descendants will be named.”{l}
He reckoned that God was able even to raise people from the dead; and figuratively speaking, he did receive Isaac back from the dead.{m}
By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau with regard to things still to come.{n}
By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, and he worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff.{o}
By faith Joseph, as his end drew near, spoke of the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his bones.{p}
By faith, when Moses was born, his parents kept him hidden three months, for they saw what a fine child he was, and they did not fear the decree of the king.{q}
By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter,{r}
choosing rather to share ill-treatment with the people of God than to enjoy the passing pleasures of sin.
He considered the reproach of the Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking ahead to the reward.{s}
By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger, for he persevered as one who sees him who is invisible.
By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of the blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch them.{t}
By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as if on dry land, but when the Egyptians attempted it, they were swallowed up.{u}
By faith the walls of Jericho fell after they had been encircled for seven days.{v}
By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had welcomed the spies in peace.{w}
And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets,{x}
Through faith they overcame kingdoms, carried out justice, gained what was promised, closed the jaws of lions,
put out raging fire, got away from the sword’s edge, found strength in weakness, grew powerful in battle, routed the armies of foreigners.
Women had their dead given back to them, raised to life. Others were tortured to death, turning down release so as to gain a better resurrection.{y}
Others again had to face jeers and whips, as well as chains and prison.
Some were stoned; some were tested; some were sawn apart; some died by the sword. They roamed about clothed in the skins of sheep and goats, in need, in distress, ill-treated,{z}
people of whom the world was not worthy, wandering in deserts and mountains and in caves and holes in the ground.
Yet none of these, though they won approval through their faith, received the promise,
because God had in view something better for us, that they should not be brought to perfection without us.

notes.text: Assurance: Greek *hypostasis*, “substance,” “firm ground,” “title deed”; compare 1:3; 3:14. *Proof*: or “conviction.”
Commended: literally “testified to,” that is, by God; so also in verses 4–5, 39.
The ages: or “the universe”; compare 1:2.
*Abel*: Hebrew *Hevel*, “breath,” “vapor.” *Cain*: Hebrew *Qayin*, explained in Gen 4:1 by the word for “acquired.” See Gen 4:3–10.
*Enoch*: Hebrew *Hanokh*, perhaps “dedicated.” Gen 5:24 in the Greek Old Testament.
*Noah*: Hebrew *Noach*, related in Gen 5:29 to a word for “comfort” or “rest.” *Took heed*: or “in reverent fear.”
*Isaac*: Hebrew *Yitschaq*, “he laughs” (Gen 17:17–19; 21:6). *Jacob*: Hebrew *Yaʿaqov*, explained in Gen 25:26; 27:36 as “heel-grabber,” “supplanter.”

*Sarah*: Hebrew, “princess” (Gen 17:15). *Sarah herself … received power to conceive*: or, as many interpreters read the Greek, “by faith he (Abraham), together with Sarah herself, received power to beget offspring.” Some manuscripts add that Sarah was barren; later manuscripts add “gave birth.”
Compare Gen 22:17; 32:12.
Strangers and exiles: compare Gen 23:4; 1 Chr 29:15; Ps 39:12.
Only son: Greek *monogenēs*, “one and only.” See Gen 22:1–14.
Gen 21:12. *Descendants*: literally “seed.”
Figuratively speaking: literally “in a parable.”
*Esau*: Hebrew, perhaps “hairy” (Gen 25:25). See Gen 27:27–40.

*Joseph*: Hebrew *Yosef*, explained in Gen 30:23–24 as “may he add.” *Leaning on the top of his staff*: Gen 47:31 in the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew vowels as traditionally read give “at the head of his bed.” See also Gen 48:8–20.
See Gen 50:24–25; Exod 13:19. *The Israelites*: literally “the sons of Israel.”

What a fine child: literally “that the child was beautiful” or “well pleasing”; compare Exod 2:2; Acts 7:20. *Edict*: compare Exod 1:22. Some later manuscripts add here a sentence about Moses killing the Egyptian.
Pharaoh: Egyptian, “great house,” the title of the king of Egypt.
The reproach of the Christ: or “the reproach of the Anointed One”; compare Ps 89:50–51.
Passover: Greek *pascha*, from Hebrew *pesach* (Exod 12:11–13, 21–23).
Red Sea: so the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew has *Yam Suph*, “Sea of Reeds” (Exod 14:21–29).
*Jericho*: Hebrew, perhaps related to the word for “moon” or “fragrance.” See Josh 6:12–21.
*Rahab*: Hebrew, “broad,” “wide.” See Josh 2:1–21; 6:22–25.

*Gideon*: Hebrew, “hewer.” *Barak*: Hebrew, “lightning.” *Samson*: Hebrew *Shimshon*, from the word for “sun.” *Jephthah*: Hebrew *Yiftach*, “he opens.” *Samuel*: Hebrew *Shemuel*, explained in 1 Sam 1:20 by the words “asked of God,” more probably “name of God.”
Compare 1 Kgs 17:17–24; 2 Kgs 4:18–37. *Tortured*: probably on the rack or drum; compare 2 Macc 6:18–7:42.

Some were tested: Greek *epeirasthēsan*. Some manuscripts omit it, and some scholars suspect an early copying error for *eprēsthēsan*, “they were burned.” *Sawn in two*: a Jewish tradition tells of Isaiah being sawn in two.

verses.text: With so vast a cloud of witnesses around us, then, let us too throw off every burden and the sin that entangles so easily, and let us run with perseverance the course laid out for us,{a}

keeping our gaze on Jesus, who leads the way in faith and brings it to completion. For the sake of the joy that lay ahead of him he bore the cross, scorning the shame, and he is seated at the right of God’s throne.{b}
Consider him who endured such hostility from sinners against themselves, so that you do not grow weary and lose heart.{c}
You have not yet, in your contest with sin, stood firm to the point of bloodshed.

for the Lord disciplines the one he loves,
and he punishes every son whom he receives.”{e}
It is for discipline that you endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline?
If you are without the discipline that all have received, you are not true sons but illegitimate.
Again, we had human fathers who corrected us, and we treated them with respect. Should we not be far more ready to submit to the Father of spirits, and so live?{f}
Our fathers corrected us for a brief time as they judged fit, but God does it for our benefit, that we may have a share in his holiness.
No discipline, while it lasts, seems a matter for joy; it is painful. Afterward, though, those who have been schooled by it reap from it a harvest of righteousness and peace.
So strengthen the hands that hang limp and the knees that give way,{g}
and make level tracks for your feet, so that the limb that is lame may not be dislocated, but may instead be healed.{h}
Strive for peace with all people, and for holiness, for apart from holiness none will see the Lord.
Watch that no one falls short of God’s grace, and that no “bitter root sprouts up to cause trouble,” poisoning many through it;{i}
that no one is sexually immoral or godless like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal.{j}
You know that later on, when he wished to receive the blessing as heir, he was turned away; he found no room for a change of mind, though he sought the blessing with tears.{k}
You have not come to what can be touched by the hand, to fire that burns, to darkness, deep gloom and storm,{l}
and the blast of a trumpet and a sound of words, such that those who heard it begged that no further message be spoken to them.
For they could not bear the command that was given: “If even an animal touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.”{m}
Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I am terrified and trembling.”{n}
But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels in festal gathering,{o}
and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect,
and to Jesus, who mediates a new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, which speaks better things than Abel’s blood.{p}
Take care not to reject the one who speaks. If those who rejected him when he gave warning on earth did not get away, much less will we, if we turn our backs on the one who warns us from heaven.
At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also heaven.”{q}
The words “Yet once more” point to the removing of things that are shaken, as things that have been made, so that the things not shaken may endure.
Therefore, since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us be grateful, and so offer to God worship that pleases him, with reverence and awe;{r}
for our God is a consuming fire.{s}

notes.text: Witnesses: Greek *martyres*, people who testify; here those whose faith is attested in chapter 11. *Clings so closely*: the meaning of the rare Greek word *euperistatos* is uncertain; perhaps “easily distracting.” One early papyrus, P46 as reported, reads “easily distracting.”
Leads the way: Greek *archēgos*, “pioneer,” “founder”; see 2:10. *For the sake of the joy*: or “instead of the joy.”
Against themselves: so the Westcott–Hort text, following Sinaiticus and other early witnesses as reported; most manuscripts read “against himself.”
Prov 3:11–12 in the Greek Old Testament. *The Lord*: the Hebrew text has *Yahweh*; so also in verse 6.

Punishes … receives: so the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew reads “as a father the son in whom he delights.” *Son*: so throughout this passage the Greek speaks of sons, but the teaching applies to all God’s children.
Human fathers: literally “fathers of our flesh.”
Prov 4:26 in the Greek Old Testament.
Deut 29:18 in the Greek Old Testament.
See Gen 25:29–34.

Room for a change of mind: literally “place of repentance,” perhaps meaning no way to change his father’s decision. *Sought the blessing*: or “sought repentance”; the Greek pronoun could refer to either. See Gen 27:30–40.
What can be touched: later manuscripts read “a mountain that can be touched.” See Exod 19:16–22; Deut 4:11; 5:22–26.
Deut 9:19.

*Zion*: Hebrew, perhaps “fortress”; the hill of Jerusalem. *Jerusalem*: Hebrew *Yerushalayim*, perhaps “foundation of Shalem” or “foundation of peace.” *Myriads*: literally “tens of thousands.” *Of angels in festal gathering*: or “of angels, to the festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn.”
Compare Gen 4:10.
Hag 2:6.
Let us be grateful: or “let us hold on to grace.”

verses.text: Let love for one another as brothers continue.{a}
Do not forget to welcome strangers, for in doing so some have had angels as their guests without realizing it.{b}
Keep in mind those in prison, as if you shared their chains, and those who are ill-treated, since you too have bodies of your own.
Let marriage be honorable in everyone’s eyes, and the bed of marriage undefiled; God will bring judgment on the sexually immoral and on adulterers.
Keep your manner of life clear of greed for money, and be satisfied with what is at hand. For he has said, “I will never let you go, nor will I ever desert you.”{c}
Remember those who led you, who told you God’s word. Look at how their lives turned out, and follow the example of their faith.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.

Do not be swept aside by teachings that are various and foreign. It is a fine thing for the heart to be made firm by grace, rather than by foods, which have brought no benefit to those who live by them.{e}
We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat.
For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest as an offering for sin are burned outside the camp.{f}
So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to make the people holy through his own blood.
Let us, then, go out to him outside the camp, bearing the reproach he bore.
We have here no city that endures; we are searching for the one still to come.
Through him let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name.{g}
And do not forget kindness and sharing, for these are the sacrifices in which God delights.

Be obedient to your leaders and defer to them, since they keep watch over your souls, knowing they must render an account. Let them do it gladly and not with sighs, for that would bring you no profit.
Keep praying for us. We are persuaded that our conscience is good, since we wish to conduct ourselves well in every way.
I especially ask you to pray, so that I may be given back to you more quickly.
Now may the God of peace, who brought up from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep by the blood of the eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus,{h}
make you complete in every good thing for doing his will, bringing about in us what pleases him, through Jesus Christ; to him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.{i}
I urge you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation, for I have written to you briefly.
You should know that our brother Timothy has been set free, and if he comes soon, I will see you with him.{j}
Give our greetings to all who lead you and to all the saints. Those from Italy greet you.{k}
Grace be with all of you.{l}

notes.text: Love … as brothers: Greek *philadelphia*.
Compare Gen 18:1–8; 19:1–3.
Deut 31:6, 8; Josh 1:5.
Ps 118:6 (117:6 in the Greek Old Testament). *The Lord*: the Hebrew text has *Yahweh*.
Foods: probably rules about clean and unclean foods or sacrificial meals.
Through him: some manuscripts add “then.” *The fruit of lips*: compare Hos 14:2 in the Greek Old Testament.
Compare Isa 63:11; Zech 9:11.
In us: some manuscripts read “in you.”
*Timothy*: Greek *Timotheos*, “honoring God.” *Set free*: or “has set out.”
Those from Italy: either people in Italy or Italians living elsewhere; the phrase does not settle where the letter was written.
With all of you: later manuscripts add “Amen.”
